samples.hyp: Assessing the required SARS-CoV-2 mass testing intensity to prevent an outbreak in Lusaka District, Zambia's capital city, considering asymptomatic individuals.
Simple mathematical modeling study

In Africa, the novel coronavirus disease (COVID-19), caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2), is believed to have asymptomatic (or mildly symptomatic) individuals playing a significant role in the spread of the infection.
The extent to which asymptomatic individuals are infectious is still not fully understood.
However, studies indicate that their administrative status is crucial for controlling the spread of SARS-CoV-2.

We developed a simple susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed (SEIR) mathematical model to explore the impact of quarantine on asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infected individuals in Lusaka District, Zambia, to control the pandemic through mass testing.
For this, we modeled two scenarios: (1) asymptomatic individuals account for approximately 70% of all COVID-19 cases, and (2) asymptomatic individuals account for only approximately 50% of all cases.

For comparison, the model was evaluated first assuming that asymptomatic individuals transmit infection at the same rate as symptomatic individuals, and second, and more likely, assuming that asymptomatic individuals transmit infection at half the rate of symptomatic individuals.

A model assuming 70% asymptomatic cases requires a minimum and consistent daily mass testing rate of ≥7911 tests/100,000 population to control the epidemic if asymptomatic individuals are half as infectious.  If equal infectiousness is assumed, a testing rate of ≥10028 tests/100,000 population would be necessary.

For 50% lower asymptomatic mass testing rates, ≥4540 tests/100,000 population of asymptomatic individuals compared to symptomatic individuals is sufficient to control the epidemic at the assumed infection transmission rate.
Discussion and Conclusion

Our model predicts that the prevalence of COVID-19 infections, including asymptomatic individuals, can be used to measure the control of SARS-CoV-2 transmission in Lusaka, Zambia, using mass testing; however, this would be very expensive.
Mass testing in large cities like Lusaka could curb the spread of COVID-19; but is this feasible?
As predicted by 2020 computer models, the spread of COVID-19 in large cities could be controlled by extensively testing people and isolating those who test positive.
However, researchers stated that this approach may be expensive and impractical.
At the beginning of the pandemic, many people infected with COVID-19 were asymptomatic but still transmitted the disease to others.
Some studies suggest that 50% to 80% of individuals with COVID-19 were asymptomatic (showing no symptoms); and they may be responsible for 40% to 70% of new infections.
Researchers wanted to know if identifying and isolating asymptomatic individuals could help control the spread of COVID-19.
Furthermore, mass testing, i.e., testing many people at once, effectively identifies asymptomatic individuals.
Researchers have developed a computer model that predicts how individuals transition from susceptibility to infection and subsequent recovery.
The study focused on data obtained from Lusaka District, Zambia, which has its own international airport, shares borders with two countries, and is a corporate center.

Four events were identified where the characteristics of COVID-19 appeared to vary geographically; in these, between 50% and 70% of COVID-19 cases were asymptomatic, and these asymptomatic cases were equally or half as infectious as symptomatic cases.
The researchers' model found that the spread of COVID-19 can be controlled by conducting mass testing and isolating positive individuals, including those without symptoms.
To reduce the maximum number of events by 90% across all events, approximately 10% of Lusaka's population would have needed to be tested daily.
Furthermore, to keep new COVID-19 infections down, approximately 22% of the population needs to be tested daily.
Although Zambia implemented numerous COVID-19 restrictions, cases appear to be increasing.
Mass testing in a small Italian town has reduced COVID-19 cases by 90%.
However, there are no previous studies indicating that it could be equally effective in another large city.

It should be noted here that the researchers did not conduct mass testing in this study; instead, they developed a model suggesting that mass testing in large cities could limit the spread of COVID-19.
However, it raised concerns that it could be very expensive.
Furthermore, they stated that it could be more effective when implemented alongside other measures such as movement restrictions, contact tracing, and vaccination.
The Zambian research suggests that asymptomatic COVID-19 cases appear to be more prevalent in Africa.
There is low generalizability of polygenic scores across African populations due to genetic and environmental heterogeneity.
The representation of African populations in genetic studies is lower than expected; however, they face high levels of genetic diversity and widespread environmental exposures globally.

Systematic evaluations of genetic prediction strategies around ancestry in diverse Africa have not yet been conducted.  Therefore, we calculated polygenic risk scores (PRS) using simulations across Africa and empirical data from South Africa, Uganda, and the UK to better understand the generalizability of genetic studies.
The accuracy of GWAS improves in related samples compared to unrelated studies.
We found that the accuracy of PCA was low for all traits among South Africans, who have high levels of genetic and ethnic diversity, but varied between groups.
Differences between African lineages contribute to the variability in pangenome accuracy, more so than other large-scale genomic differences between individuals in Uganda and the UK.

Using currently available European-only genetic studies, we inferred the P. falciparum genetic lineages in Africa. The high diversity observed yielded the highest accuracy in identifying hemoglobin and white blood cell count variations, reflecting a large impact of population stratification on genes known to influence sickle cell anemia and allergic responses, respectively.
The variation in the accuracy of PCA among African populations from different regions is comparable to that among non-African continental populations, suggesting comparable diversity.
The reason we cannot accurately predict genetic diseases in people of African descent.
Researchers say that current methods for predicting whether someone will develop a genetic disease do not work well for people of African descent.
This is because the database behind such predictions largely reflects the genes of people of European descent.
The dbGaP database refers to “Database of Genotypes and Phenotypes,” which scientists use to search for the genetic basis of diseases.
Indeed, a polygenic risk score (PRS) can be used to calculate an individual's genetic susceptibility to disease or risk.
However, the majority of the genomic data comes from individuals of European ancestry.
In this study, researchers sought to determine how well the calculation of genetic disease risks using PRS works for people of African ancestry.
Furthermore, they wanted to see if a more diverse database, in other words, a database that included more African genetic information, would improve predictions.
Scientifically, this calculation is known as “polygenic risk score” or PRS.

Computers were used to calculate and predict the genetic risks of African populations using GWAS, and African medical records were used to see if specific traits or diseases were present due to changes in genes.
For most traits, people found that genetic risk scores from European ancestry individuals yielded more accurate results when compared to those from African ancestry.
As mentioned, the risk effects in African populations are much lower, due to high diversity within the population; this is inconsistent with what we see in European populations.
Furthermore, they state that the accuracy of the PCA increases as the contribution from Africa decreases.
Ethiopian populations with greater genetic similarity to European populations had better predictions for genetic diseases.
The predictive accuracy was improved when a more diverse SNP panel, including individuals of African descent, was used.
Predicting blood diseases was particularly accurate.

Previous studies have shown that the polygenic risk score (PRS) is low for African populations; this means that the genomic risk score database predicts a lower genetic risk for individuals of African descent.
But we know this is not actually true.

This study explains that these low genetic risk scores are due to the underrepresentation of African genomes in the GWAS database; therefore, current PRS values are not accurate in predicting genetic diseases in Africa.
Researchers suggest that using a broader database that includes genetic information from people of African descent would be beneficial.
Therefore, further work is needed to expand the GWA studies to include African ancestries to accurately predict the risk of genetic diseases among African populations.
The authors of this study were from Africa, the USA, and the UK.
Evaluation of visual inspection and screening for the prevention of cervical cancer and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia in Namibia.
Approximately 851,340 women in Namibia are at risk of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, which can cause cervical cancer.
Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) and cryotherapy have proven to be highly effective.
However, data regarding cervical cancer screening programs are lacking.
This study evaluated visual and cytological screening for the prevention of cervical cancer and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) in Namibia.
The findings showed that women with HPV, cervicitis, koilocytosis, and atypia are at a significantly higher risk of being VIA positive.
Specifically, older women with HIV have a higher risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
VIA screening seems to work, but in the Namibian context, colposcopy should be improved and used in conjunction with positive HR-HPV results for better patient follow-up.
Methods incorporating HPV screening for different age groups and at-risk populations (e.g., HIV positive, autoimmune disease) are recommended.

The screening process can be further improved by using an intervention model that utilizes previous test results, incorporating women's health goals, updated knowledge, and practices that align with the country's context.
Namibian women at risk of cervical cancer should be screened and treated promptly.
Many studies show that women are at risk for cervical cancer, but routine screening practices in Namibia do not always reflect the utilization of these tests.
Researchers recommend regular screenings to detect warning signs early, which could save women from contracting the deadly disease.
Cervical cancer (cancer of the lower part of the uterus) claims the lives of many women worldwide.
One of the main causes of cervical cancer is the human papillomavirus, or HPV.
HPV is a virus that infects the cells of the cervix, causing lesions called lesions that can develop into cancer over time.
Although an HPV vaccine exists to prevent HPV, many women in Africa, including Namibia, cannot access it.
This means that testing for the presence of the virus or lesions is crucial, especially for these women, as it is the best way to prevent cancer.
Researchers of this study argue that hospitals need accurate guidelines and information to know which diagnostic test to use.
Also, healthcare workers stated that they need more information to understand how factors such as age and health affect women's risk of contracting HPV and cancer.
The study investigated the effectiveness of commonly used screening methods for detecting HPV and lesions.
They also wanted to compare screening methods; for example, testing for damage by collecting cells from the cervix instead of looking for subtle lesions.
Furthermore, they wanted to know if other factors among women, such as age and the presence of other diseases like HIV, would modify their susceptibility to HPV or cancer.
Knowing this information could help hospitals and clinics to use screening methods more effectively.
Researchers reviewed the records of 214 female patients screened and treated for HPV, lesions, and cervical cancer at a Windhoek, Namibia hospital.
Specifically, it focused on early-stage cervical cancer, which can be treated easily and effectively.
Information on each woman's age and general health status was also collected.
Reviewing these records revealed that different screening methods provided clinicians with different information and may be more useful before or after HPV progression to cancer.
For example, cancer is most often detected by collecting and examining cervical cells.
However, lesions were mostly detected by visual inspection alone, using a method called Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA).
The advantage of this technique is that it allows doctors to obtain lesions cheaply and quickly.
This is because it still uses common instruments used in women's gynecological examinations, such as a speculum (a metal instrument used to examine the vagina).
It was found that using multiple methods, especially repeated screenings, generally provided doctors with more information about women's risk of developing cancer.
Furthermore, the researchers found that older women with HIV have a significantly higher risk of developing cancer.
Researchers also reported that very few women had been screened for HPV (before seeking lesions) even if the tests were accessible.
This could be a crucial way to detect the disease much earlier.
Overall, their results suggest that the Namibian healthcare system needs to plan more carefully to detect HPV and cervical cancer early using cost-effective screening methods.
The study was conducted in collaboration with scientists from Namibia and South Africa.
In the South African cohort, HBV/HIV co-infection compared to HBV mono-infection.

To determine the clinical impact and improve clinical care based on selected targets for global hepatitis B virus (HBV) elimination, we planned to distinguish individuals with HBV mono-infection from those with HBV/HIV co-infection.
We report observational data from 115 adults with chronic hepatitis B infection (CHB) from the University of Cape Town Hospital, South Africa, a subset of a larger, real-world, cross-sectional study.
HIV co-infection was found in 39 (34%) of the individuals.
A large cross-sectional population study recorded clinical and laboratory data.

Compared to individuals with HIV co-infection, adults with HBV mono-infection had a lower tendency to be HBeAg-positive (p=0.01), to undergo elastography (p<0.0001), and to be on antiretroviral therapy (p<0.0001). Conversely, they showed a higher tendency to have detectable HBV viraemia (p=0.04) and moderate/severe liver disease manifestations including thrombocytopenia (p=0.007), elevated bilirubin (p=0.004), and higher APRI score (p=0.02).
All three hepatocellular carcinoma cases occurred in the context of HBV monoinfection.

Our data suggests that individuals with HBV infection alone may experience worse outcomes compared to those with HIV co-infection. This highlights potential systemic inequities in referral, follow-up, and treatment.
Researchers provide guidance to improve Hepatitis B treatment.
In a recent study, researchers found that co-infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) may offer benefits for treating HBV-only infection.
Co-infection with both HBV and HIV is a serious problem in South Africa.
Doctors need to understand how these viruses work, how the medications used to treat them are used, and their interactions in order to better diagnose and treat patients.
Researchers sought to determine the impact of treatment on patients with HBV alone compared to those with both HBV and HIV.
For this study, the researchers recruited 115 adult patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB).
Those recruited were from the Cape Town Tygerberg Hospital in South Africa.
Some patients were co-infected with HIV (39), while others were infected only with HBV.
The researchers surveyed race, age, and sex, and conducted numerous clinical and laboratory tests.
They found that patients with only HBV had a lower tendency to take anti-HIV medication, and also showed natural signs of liver disease (this is because the HBV virus can cause severe liver disease).

Researchers showed that individuals infected only with HBV may experience worse outcomes compared to those co-infected with HIV and HBV. This is because patients infected with both viruses are more likely to receive antiretroviral therapy for HIV, which offers some benefits in combating HBV infection.
The results from this study show that options for referral, follow-up, and treatment of HBV have a relatively greater benefit for those with HIV and HBV co-infection compared to those with HBV alone.
Researchers stated that we should improve the provision of safe and equitable services for patients infected only with HBV.
One limitation of this study was the small sample size, which was restricted to a single country and its hospital system.
Some contemporary hospital practices may offer a contrasting perspective to this study.
Further studies may be needed to accurately identify the variations found in this study.
This paper demonstrates the high potential for collaboration with researchers from South Africa and the United Kingdom working on this project.
The use of South African patients for this study makes it relevant to a specific African population.
Furthermore, this study could be used to formulate better treatment plans for patients suffering from HBV, HIV, or both.
Assessment of the Impact of Insecurity on Women's Entrepreneurial Activities in the Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State

This study examines the impact of insecurity on women's entrepreneurial activities in the Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State, focusing specifically on women's financial dependence, the types of collaborative entrepreneurial activities among them, and the influence of insecurity on entrepreneurial efforts.
A survey was conducted on 377 women, which showed that women in Shiroaro have a high degree of financial independence and are largely entrepreneurs engaged in small and micro enterprises.

The study further showed that while a lack of security negatively impacted women's entrepreneurial activity in the form of capital loss or decline, there was no significant decline in the number of women entrepreneurs.

The study recommended the creation of sustainable programs to improve women's access to and use of financial services, and the creation and strengthening of community-based policing organizations to address the lack of security in the study area.
Female traders in Niger need more security.
Researchers found that while businesswoman in Niger are highly entrepreneurial and financially independent, they face challenges in accessing security from criminals.

Researchers wanted to determine the level of safety experienced by women running businesses in the Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State, and how this impacts their businesses and financial independence.
377 women in this area were interviewed about their entrepreneurial activities, financial dependence, and the challenges they faced regarding their safety and security.
Of the women, 43% reported not being financially dependent on men, while 32% reported being financially dependent on others.
Researchers found that about 85% of women earned income from various businesses, while only a few reported relying on salaries.
About 56% derive income from farming, and 79% from business.
About one in five women earns money by braiding, weaving, twisting, or washing hair.
Most women (91%), according to their statements to the researchers, reported that their businesses had been negatively impacted by fear of attacks from thieves and criminals.
As a result of these attacks, they lose money and even their husbands, sometimes forcing them to raise their children alone.
The women also stated that they lacked sufficient skills and capital to expand their businesses.
Despite these challenges, researchers reported that Nigerien women continued to perform well in their businesses.
He stated that Shirooro has people from various tribes and religions, and that this is good for business.
This study contradicts the findings of other researchers who reported that women's involvement in household care is associated with lower business success.
Instead, these researchers argue that the success of female traders in this Nigerien area is largely impacted by the threat of attacks from criminals and thieves.
The researchers recommended that all stakeholders must collaboratively address the challenges hindering business success.
For example, women in Niger should have greater access to financial support, agriculture, and security.
It was also suggested that women engaged in business could create groups to help combat thieves and criminals.
Maternal serum concentrations of selenium, copper, and zinc during pregnancy are associated with preterm birth: A case-control study in Malawi.
Preterm birth is defined as giving birth before completing 37 weeks of gestation.
A study was conducted to assess the association between selenium, copper, and zinc concentrations in maternal blood and preterm birth.
In this cross-sectional study, 181 pregnant women participated; of these, 90 (49.7%) delivered at term, while 91 (50.3%) experienced preterm birth.

Generally speaking, the selenium concentration in the liver was 77.0; SD 19.4 µg/L, copper 2.50; SD 0.52 mg/L, and zinc 0.77; SD 0.20 mg/L, respectively, relative to the initial values of 47-142 µg/L, 0.76-1.59 mg/L, and 0.59-1.11 mg/L.
The results show that there was no deficiency of selenium and zinc during pregnancy;  nor was there a high accumulation of copper in the placenta.
Prenatal exposure was associated with copper and zinc accumulation in maternal liver.
Zinc, copper, and selenium levels associated with pregnancy.

Researchers found high concentrations of the micronutrients selenium, copper, and zinc in women who had experienced preterm birth. However, it is not yet known whether these high concentrations originated from their diet.
Preterm birth occurs when a woman gives birth before completing 37 weeks of pregnancy.
It is associated with adverse health outcomes ranging from birth defects affecting the fetus to death.
Although many factors may contribute to preterm birth, the role of high levels of micronutrients in diet and environment is relatively unknown.
Although these micronutrients are essential for child development, researchers want to understand what might happen when they are abundant.

For this study, researchers planned to measure the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc in women who experienced preterm birth, to determine the extent to which these micronutrients were associated with the risk of preterm birth.
Researchers collected blood samples from 181 women immediately after delivery at two hospitals in Lilongwe, the capital city of Malawi, between June 2016 and February 2017.
Blood samples were sent to a laboratory in Norway.  After separating the serum (or unadulterated blood), the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc were measured.
Of the 181 women included in the study, half experienced preterm birth; in these, researchers found high levels of selenium, copper, and zinc.

Furthermore, in addition to micronutrients, they adjusted their calculations to account for other factors suspected of contributing to preterm birth, such as age, overall health status, and obstetric history.
They concluded that high levels of selenium and copper do not play a significant role in causing preterm birth, but that high levels of zinc increase the risk of preterm birth by six times.
However, the presence of copper, known for its toxic effects, at high levels was a concern for the researchers.
This study, which was supposed to involve 600 women, was conducted on only 181 women; this limited the researchers' ability to adequately identify problems associated with high selenium levels.
To identify potential sources of these three-minute meals, participants' daily dietary habits were not investigated, nor was body mass index (BMI) data collected.
This is the first study of its kind to measure the effects of selenium, copper, and zinc on pregnant women in Malawi.

Africa is one of the places with the highest rates of preterm birth.  Compared to Western countries where it occurs in 5%, it is at 18% in Africa. Therefore, researchers want to know if diet plays a role in this.
Homing behavior of the pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri), site fidelity, and territoriality in Kenya
Animals exhibit unique spatial and temporal behaviors that enhance their survival.
Understanding such characteristics is a crucial step towards effective conservation and management, especially for endangered species.

In this study, we investigated the homing ability of pancake tortoises when translocated and also examined the species' site fidelity and territoriality within their natural habitats in Kitui County, Kenya.

The behavior of 39 tortoises inhabiting 12 isolated rocky outcrop sites was studied using a combination of radio tracking, camera trapping, and group-level scat and ad libitum sampling from July 2020 to June 2022.
Fourteen of the turtles were fitted with radio transmitters, and their movements and behavior were monitored as they moved between crevices in their habitat.

Except for two females that had successfully adapted to their new cracks, all other eels attempted to return to their home cracks; 46.15% successfully returned to their home crack, while 15.38% reached areas believed to be within their home range.
Successful return migration provides evidence of strong site fidelity within the species.

Analysis of turtle crack occupancy showed no statistically significant difference in the average number of turtles present in cracks (F(1,22) = 0.0699, P>0.05) over 162 sample days, supporting the presence of strong site fidelity within the species.

On the other hand, observations of camera trapping events and *Ad libitum* samples confirmed that male pancake tortoises are highly territorial, aggressively defending their territories from other approaching males.
Lost pancake tortoises have a remarkable ability to 'find their way home'.
Researchers studying the behavior of East African pancake tortoises (Malacochersus tornieri) have made a surprising discovery: the animals can find their way back home after traveling long distances.
Understanding how and why they do this could be important for the conservation of these rare animals.
This homing behavior exhibited by these turtles is called "natal homing," and many other animals can also do it.
The ability to return to specific locations allows animals to return to food, mates, and shelter, improving their chances of survival and reproduction.

Although the homing behavior of migrating sea and freshwater turtles has been studied, researchers in this study state that very little is known about homing in tortoises (terrestrial turtle counterparts).
In this study, the researchers aim to better understand the behavior of pancake tortoises in their natural habitat within Kenya's arid regions.
They studied the animals as they moved and fed, and as they went to crevices or gaps in the rock to rest.
Researchers observed groups of pancake tortoises for approximately two years and set up cameras to record video of the animals when they were not being observed.
Furthermore, radio transmitters were attached to 14 of the eels.
These researchers use small devices to track animal movement and where they spend their time during the day and night.
Then, to facilitate easier study, the researchers relocated some of these monitored turtles to a new location.
What surprised the researchers, however, was that two of the tortoises began to return to their territories, which were located between 1 and 2.5 km from where they had been collected.
This was the time the researchers decided to move many animals from their habitats to see if they showed similar 'return migration' behavior.
Surprisingly, about half of the turtles were able to return to the same cracks they had occupied before relocation, often traveling more than 1.5 kilometers to do so.
The remaining 15% were able to return to the general area, but could not locate their original capture point.
Researchers also found that various cracks mostly housed the same number of tortoises, suggesting that the tortoises consistently use the same resting spots.
Camera recordings showed that the male tortoises are territorial, meaning they fight off other males attempting to enter their territory or burrow.

Researchers stated that this is the first time that homing behavior has been observed in pancake tortoises, and their results show that these animals prefer to stay and rest in one place as much as possible.
Their study does not explain how the eels find their way back to their natal habitat, so future research should focus on understanding this crucial point.
Because animals sometimes need to be moved to new habitats for conservation purposes, this information will help conservationists ensure the safety of the animals in their new habitat.
The study, a collaboration between scientists from Kenya and China, adds to our understanding of homing behavior in elephants and other animals.
High-dose oral and intravenous rifampicin plasma pharmacokinetics in patients with tuberculous meningitis:
Randomized controlled trial
High-dose intravenous rifampicin may improve outcomes for tuberculous meningitis, but is not feasible in high-pressure settings.

We hypothesize that plasma rifampicin susceptibility will be similar between oral administration of 35 mg/kg body weight and intravenous administration of 20 mg/kg, as tested for efficacy in tuberculous meningitis.
We conducted a randomized, parallel-group pharmacokinetic study of intensified anti-tuberculosis treatment in a clinical trial for tuberculous meningitis.
Participants with tuberculosis (TB) and HIV were recruited from South African hospitals and randomly assigned to one of three rifampicin treatment groups.
Standard (oral 10 mg/kg), high dose (oral 35 mg/kg), and intravenous (20 mg/kg).
An enhanced pharmacokinetic sampling was performed on day 3.
The data were analyzed using unstratified analyses, and exposures were compared using geometric mean ratios (GMRs).
Forty-six participants received pharmacokinetic sampling (normal dose, n = 17; high-dose oral, n = 15; intravenous, n = 14).
The median CD4 count was 130 cells/mm³ (interquartile range [IQR], 66–253 cells/mm³).

The geometric mean area under the concentration-time curve from 0 to 24 hours (AUC0-24) for rifampicin was 42.9 mg·h/ml (95% confidence interval [CI], 24.5 to 75.0 mg·h/ml) for the standard oral dose, 295.2 mg·h/ml (95% CI, 189.9 to 458.8 mg·h/ml) for the high oral dose, and 206.5 mg·h/ml (95% CI, 154.6 to 275.8 mg·h/ml) for the intravenous dose.
The rifampicin AUC0-24 GMR was 1.44 (90% CI, 0.84 to 2.21), and the maximum observed serum concentration (Cmax) GMR was 0.89 (90% CI, 0.63 to 1.23) for oral relative to intravenous administration.

The plasma rifampicin AUC0-24 after oral administration of a 35-mg/kg dose was greater than that after intravenous administration of a 20-mg/kg dose during the first few days of tuberculosis (TB) treatment.
The findings support the use of oral rifampicin in future tuberculosis meningitis trials.
High doses of pills can be tested for HIV patients with tuberculous meningitis.
Researchers have determined that it is worthwhile to begin investigating whether a high dose of rifampicin can cure HIV-positive patients with tuberculosis.
Up to 3 out of 5 HIV patients with tuberculosis die from this disease, which also affects the nervous system.
Survivors suffer permanent damage to their central nervous system and to the crucial nerves emanating from the brain.
This could affect their emotions and movements.
Some patients experience falls, stroke, or paralysis of their face or limbs.
Rifampicin, a potent antibiotic used to prevent tuberculosis, is routinely administered in pill form to kill the tuberculosis bacteria.
Severely ill patients often have difficulty swallowing pills.
Rifampicin can also be administered intravenously (into the veins) in liquid form.
The fluid is administered intravenously to the patient to release it into the body.
No studies have yet been conducted to determine how a patient's body processes the medication when this method is used.
Blood-based treatments require additional equipment, hospitalization, and a trained healthcare professional who knows how to properly administer injections.
Therefore, it is not necessarily an alternative in resource-limited settings.
Doctors know that rifampicin does not readily penetrate the cerebrospinal fluid, where bacteria may hide in the brain, spinal cord, and skull.
This is why a high dose (doses) is needed to effectively kill all bacteria in the patient's body.
However, researchers were not certain how high a dose could be both effective and safe.

Researchers from South Africa and the United Kingdom wanted to determine, using a small number of patients, whether high-dose rifampicin administration, either orally or intravenously, is safe and how the body handles each route of administration.
Other researchers need to know this before initiating large trials or tests that plan to administer high doses of rifampicin to many patients.
One of three rifampicin treatment regimens was given to 46 HIV-positive South African patients with tuberculous meningitis.
The initial standard treatment currently given to patients is 10 mg of rifampicin per kilogram of the patient's weight.
The other group received tablets with a maximum dose of 35 milligrams per kilogram of patient weight.
The third group received 20 milligrams per kilogram of body weight intravenously.
Blood samples were taken from the patients after three days.
The researchers measured the amount of rifampicin in the blood plasma (the liquid component of blood).
Higher concentrations of rifampicin were found in the bodies of patients given the drug intravenously or in higher than standard doses compared to those taking standard doses.
The drug concentration in blood plasma is similar to that of a high dose and intravenous administration.
These levels were high even when patients received only the standard dose.
According to the researchers, this indicates that increasing the dosage of rifampicin may improve the health of patients suffering from tuberculous meningitis.
It doesn't matter whether they are taken as pills or intravenously – the main thing is that they are received in high doses, because their bodies can accumulate high concentrations.
The results support findings from trials conducted in Uganda and Indonesia.
For example, two small trials in Indonesia have suggested that high doses of rifampicin, administered orally or intravenously, may improve survival in many patients.
Unfortunately, researchers caution that the lower than expected number of participants involved in this study at its outset may affect the results.
The study was conducted in South Africa.
The plan supports conducting trials to test the efficacy of administering high-dose rifampicin to HIV patients with tuberculous meningitis.
It is anticipated that such treatment will save the lives of many people in Africa and other parts of the world where tuberculous meningitis is a major problem.
Can the combined use of biochar and fertilizer significantly improve the quality of highly weathered coastal savanna soil?
Soil fertility decline in sub-Saharan Africa is a major constraint to crop production.
Many authors have reported that adding biochar and fertilizer has a negative impact on soil fertility.

This study conducted a 30-day laboratory incubation experiment using 120 g samples.  Haplic Argisols were amended with corn stover biochar (Bio), rice husk biochar (RBio), coconut shell biochar (Coco300 and Coco700), poultry litter compost (Compost), a rice husk biochar-compost mixture (RCOComp), or a corn stover biochar-compost mixture (CocoComp), respectively, at a 1% w/w amendment:soil ratio.

Other treatments included in the study were poultry manure compost and maize straw biochar or rice husk biochar (1% compost + 1% biochar: 1% soil w/w).  This was to investigate their effects on basic soil respiration, soil pH, soil microbial carbon, cation exchange capacity, total organic carbon and total nitrogen, and available nitrogen content.
Compared to the unamended control sample, biochar and fertilizer, applied individually or together, increased soil pH by 0.28 to 2.29 pH units.

Compared to the unamended control sample, the yield was significantly higher with the sole application of biochar, or with the application of matured rice husk or maize stover biochar, or with a mixture of biochar and fertilizer. This was similar to the treatment using only biochar.
The TOC in the single biochar and the combined biochar and fertilizer treatments were 37% and 117% higher, respectively, compared to the control sample.
Adding a mixture of rice husk biochar and fertilizer increased MBC by 132% compared to the control sample, while adding fertilizer alone increased MBC by 247%.

Overall, the study showed that adding fertilizer and biochar, either separately or in combination, or using matured biochar improved the following soil parameters: soil pH and MBC, and soil bulk density and TOC; it also reduced soil C loss through basic respiration.
Biochar and fertilizer improve soil quality for crops.
This study investigated how biochar is produced from discarded biomass and is a highly porous and carbon-rich material that could be used to improve soil quality in Sub-Saharan Africa.
The study found that biochar can improve soil quality equally well as other much more expensive and less readily available options.
One of the main challenges facing crop production in sub-Saharan Africa is soil degradation.
Improved soil quality leads to better crop yields. This reduces rural poverty and mitigates the depletion of natural resources.
The research showed that biochar, a highly porous and carbon-rich material, can be used to improve soil fertility.
Biochar is a byproduct obtained by heating organic matter or biomass in the absence or with low levels of oxygen.

To stop female genital mutilation, we must first understand why it occurs.
Female genital mutilation (FGM), the cutting or removal of a girl's genitalia, is still carried out illegally or clandestinely in countries such as Kenya, Ethiopia, and Indonesia.
Researchers say that understanding why this happens is key to stopping this harmful practice and preventing the psychological and health problems that women consequently experience.
Female genital mutilation (FGM), sometimes known as female circumcision, is still commonly practiced in certain parts of Africa and Asia.
Many people have the misconception that FGM promotes hygiene and makes girls more marriageable (pure and submissive), and ensures that they will bear children.
Scientific evidence indicates that FGM is not necessary for these issues.
However, in many cases, children subjected to FGM experience numerous health complications as they age, including harmful infections, difficulty urinating (dysuria), and psychological problems.
Because the practice is extremely harmful and violates the human rights of girls, many countries have outlawed it, but people still perform it secretly.
In this study, researchers sought to understand why FGM occurs in different countries and to explore people's beliefs about the practice.
Therefore, data on FGM was collected in Kenya, Ethiopia, and Indonesia.
In each country, researchers interviewed a range of people, including parents, young people, traditional leaders, healthcare workers, and ‘cutters’ (older women who perform FGM on young girls).
In some cases, they conducted individual interviews with these people, and also held group discussions with many people, including young adults and adolescents who had suffered from FGM.
Researchers found that the reasons for FGM, the way it is performed, and beliefs about the practice vary across countries.
Furthermore, it was found that many people still use them in places where they are illegal.

For example, in Indonesia, people practicing traditional circumcision use a needle or blade to cut a specific part of the clitoris (a body part used to bring sexual satisfaction to women) when a baby girl turns 40 days old.
People believe this is necessary to ‘avoid fornication’ as well as for religious reasons.
In Ethiopia, FGM was traditionally performed early, sometimes when children were only seven days old.
Researchers found that people there believe this ensures the girl will one day become a "good wife," obedient to her husband and not aggressive.
Also, many people believed that FGM facilitates childbirth, but on the contrary, it makes childbirth more difficult.
Meanwhile, FGM signifies that a girl has reached womanhood, and it is usually performed after she reaches adolescence.
However, in some cases, women undergo FGM as young as 8 years old, and many girls become pregnant during adolescence because they are considered ready for sexual intercourse after FGM.
Researchers say their findings show that there are various reasons why FGM is still practiced.
As laws and social norms change, so do the how and where of their enforcement.
For example, parents might try to secretly arrange a marriage, even if it is illegal, because they may believe it is necessary for their daughter to be healthy and find a good husband.
This is important to recognize because in some places FGM is illegal, research on the topic can be difficult, and people may not always give truthful answers about it.

In addition to future criminalization, researchers suggest that governments and health officials should aim to stop FGM by correcting people's misconceptions about the practice and educating them about its dangers.

This study was a collaboration between scientists in Ethiopia, Indonesia, and the Netherlands, and is part of a large project called the ‘SI DU Programme’ aimed at reducing adolescent pregnancies, child marriage, and FGM.

Exposure to sodium metavanadate resulted in reproductive hormone imbalances, germ cell apoptosis, abnormal sperm characteristics and morphology, and ultrastructural changes in the testes of African giant pouched rats (Cricetomys gambianus, Waterhouse, 1840).
Recently, there has been an increase in local vanadium exposure.
This metal host is known for its toxicity.
The present study was conducted to investigate the reproductive toxicity of sodium metavanadate (SMV) in African giant pouched rats.
A 1 kg 3 mg dose of somatropin was administered daily via intramuscular injection for 14 consecutive days.
Clean water was provided to the control group.
Following treatment with So.Me.Va, we analyzed seminal hormones, sperm count and quality, and ultrastructural changes in the testes.
Our results show that the progesterone level was statistically increased in the group exposed to the virus, but the levels of testosterone, FSH, and LH were decreased.

Similarly, the group treated with SAHA showed a statistically significant decrease in sperm motility and mass movement, along with an increase in the percentage of abnormal sperm morphology and forms, and a proliferation of p53-positive cells.
Ultrastructural studies showed germ cell and Sertoli cell damage, as well as the formation of cellular and nuclear debris;  hypertrophied cells and the formation of giant cells were also observed.
Severe degeneration of the seminiferous tubules, sloughing and shedding of germ cells, and apoptotic cell death of Leydig, Sertoli, and germ cells were observed.

In summary, in utero exposure to SARS-CoV-2 can severely negatively impact some reproductive hormones, reduce sperm count and quality, induce apoptosis of Leydig, Sertoli, and germ cells, and cause testicular changes; this can lead to infertility.
Researchers have found that iron in polluted air can impair host mice.
Researchers have found that vanadium, a type of metal host, impairs the ability of mice cells to create offspring (fertility).

This study suggests that further research is needed to determine whether the increased presence of arsenic in our atmosphere due to pollution could have similar negative effects on human health, as this metalloid is toxic to humans.
Although vanadium is not a fossil fuel, it can enter the atmosphere in small amounts when fossil fuels such as oil and coal are burned.
As the world uses these fuel sources more, the amount of vanadium pollution increases.
We previously knew that those exposed to it could suffer from health problems such as anemia, dry throat and eyes, and chest pain.
Scientists have also recently shown interest in understanding the effects of vanadium on fruit productivity.
These effects were begun to be studied in mice, which are frequently used in laboratories due to their similarities to humans.
In this study, scientists were interested in determining the effect of vanadium on a common type of rat known as the African giant rat in West Africa.
They wanted to understand how vanadium affects the male rat reproductive system, specifically the sperm, hormones, testes, and cells.
Researchers injected six male mice once daily with vanadium for 14 days.
Simultaneously, another 6 mice were injected with water as a control experiment.
Because there was no chance that the water would affect the mice, the researchers could be certain that any changes they observed in the first six mice were the result of the vanadium injection.
After 14 days, they checked whether hormone levels, such as testosterone, had changed, examined their testes, and counted their sperm.
Using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) techniques, we were able to visualize in detail the changes that occurred in the male germ cells down to the individual cell level.
Researchers found that mice exposed to vanadium had significantly lower levels of testosterone and other hormones important for fertility.
Furthermore, vanadium-exposed mice had significantly lower sperm counts and reduced sperm health.
Researchers observed, for example, that some mice had headless sperm and curved tails, and that their sperm did not move as much as that of the control mice.
Since male gametes are male reproductive cells that function to fertilize female gametes, these changes make it difficult for the mice to successfully reproduce.
Finally, the researchers found that some cells from the male mice's testes were severely damaged or destroyed by vanadium.
Researchers stated that the changes they found could eventually lead to complete infertility.
They indicated that animals exposed to vanadium and other pollutants in the atmosphere may suffer reproductive failure and could potentially become extinct due to these effects.
Because humans are mammals, like mice, scientists should also study the potential negative impacts of vanadium-contaminated areas on human health.

Researchers cautioned that further work is needed to understand the harm caused by vanadium, as some of the changes they observed in the animals' bodies and hormones differed from those found in previous scientific studies.
This study, a collaboration between scientists from Nigeria and Egypt, adds to scientists' understanding of how animals and potentially humans are affected by pollution.
Traditional uses of home gardens among indigenous communities in Northwest Ethiopia.
In general, there has been limited research attention on the spatial structure of home gardens, particularly in the Gozamin district of Northwest Ethiopia.
The main objective of this research is to better understand the floral structure and traditional uses of homegrown vegetables.
A stratified random sampling procedure was used based on the agro-ecological variation in the selected kebeles.

Home garden data was collected by dividing the gardens into four quadrats. The first quadrat extended 10 meters from the farmer's house. The second quadrat extended from 10m to 20m, the third from 20m to 30m, and the fourth quadrat, depending on the size of the garden and using the farmer's house as a reference point, extended laterally from 30m to 40m.
A semi-structured interview was used to record the informant's knowledge of vegetable varieties.
In total, 238 traditional vegetable varieties were identified from 81 households.
Of these, 39% were herbs, 29% shrubs, and 6% trees.
Biennials comprised the largest proportion (83%) of the species sampled, while annuals made up the remainder (17%).
Most species belonged to the Poaceae family, with about 22 later replaced by Fabaceae, which had 21; Asteraceae had 15.

Of the registered plants, 140 (58.6%) were species used for environmental purposes; 84 (35%) were cereal food crops; 83 (34.7%) were medicinal plant species; 39 (16.3%) were fodder species; 57 (23.8%) were plants used for material purposes; 60 (25%) were fuel wood species; 50 (21%) were plants used for social services; and 1 (0.4%) was poisonous.
Direct matrix ranking showed that *Cordia africana* was found to be a versatile, culturally important plant in the area, and was found to be highly threatened after *Ficus sur*.
The highest value of Cordia africana was for construction, while the lowest was for medicinal purposes.
The Sørensen similarity index was less than 0.5 for 64 of the sites studied.
The results showed that home gardens are diverse and productive long-term farming systems.
The traditional knowledge of indigenous communities regarding food security and biodiversity conservation in relation to their home gardens will receive continued support.
The low similarity/high diversity of species between localities indicated high species diversity in the area, likely due to differences in archaeological contexts between localities.
Ethiopian home gardens support food security and conservation.
Researchers say that many Ethiopians cultivate cereals, ornamental plants, medicinal plants, fodder crops, and plants for shade or hedging in their home gardens.
These vegetable gardens were surveyed to assess their importance in ensuring food security and environmental protection.
Communities around the world cultivate gardens for food, income generation, and other cultural purposes.
Botanical gardens conserve useful vegetables that are largely absent or disappearing in other areas.
There is little research on what Ethiopian communities definitively cultivate in their gardens.
Researchers in this study sought to investigate the types of vegetables grown in home gardens and their uses by people in the Gozamin district of Northwest Ethiopia.
Vegetables were identified and counted in 357 local gardens.
Community members were interviewed about their reasons for using the vegetables.
Researchers found that the size of vegetable gardens in Gozamin was less than a hectare.
238 different vegetables were identified, collected and classified.
Most (83%) of the vegetables were harvested year-round, with only a few (17%) being seasonal.
Their results showed that the community used vegetables for food, medicine, fodder (animal feed), and other traditional uses.
Most vegetables provided a single benefit.
For example, the large-leaved tree of the north can be used for medicine, ornamentation, food, shade, fuel, and other traditional purposes.
More than half (59%) of the plants were used for environmental purposes, serving as fences, windbreaks, shelters, and ornamentation.
The researchers stated that this helped to protect the area.
Washing vegetables also helped preserve the farm produce.
Slightly more than one-third (35%) of the vegetables were harvested for use in foods such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and spices.
However, they stated that local gardens primarily produced fruits.

Researchers reported that approximately 35% of plants were used for traditional medicine for humans and animals, while 21% served religious and ceremonial purposes, or were used for cigarettes, perfumes, and baking.
Some vegetables (17%) served as fodder for cattle, sheep, and donkeys.
The remaining 24% were used for construction materials, gardening tools, roof repairs, and rope making.
It was reported that the majority of the rural community uses firewood, thus about 25% of the trees were used for that purpose.
Researchers reported that only one (0.4%) case was identified as having the intention of using vegetables for poisoning.
Furthermore, the distribution of vegetables in the area was influenced by local factors such as people's food preferences, family finances, and market demands.
For example, Wenka, an area near the capital with irrigation water, had many vegetable gardens and recorded 130 different vegetables.
The Wenka people also supplied fruits and vegetables to the city market.
Finally, researchers stated that most farmers choose to cultivate vegetables with high benefits.
The researchers stated that their results confirm that farmers indeed cultivated a high number of diverse vegetable types on their plots for various benefits.
While these researchers found that most farmers cultivated spices, other researchers reported that trees were more common in the area.
The researchers of this study were based at Ethiopian universities.
